Bone Tool Diversity During the Stone Age: More Insights into the Human Story

Abstract

Once thought to signal the emergence of 'modern human behavior’ in the archaeological record, recent research in parts of Africa, Eurasia, and Oceania has pushed back the timeline of when bone tool technology is thought to have originated and highlighted the sophistication of this ancient and global technology. From the unworked implements used by African hominins to gather subterranean foods, to the simple pointed tools that facilitated long-distance migration of peoples into colder climates, to the sophisticated use of bone by archaic and modern humans as a canvas to express appreciation of form and harness sound—the literature on this topic is expanding every year as discoveries from new excavations and long-curated collections are reported. Seldom, however, do we find in the literature a comprehensive perspective of the sheer diversity of functions to which bone was put in the Stone Age (and synonymous Paleolithic or Pleistocene) period. In this contribution, we present a global review of the diverse range of roles that bone tools played during the period from the Middle Pleistocene to the Early to Mid Holocene (c. 8,000 years ago). Our aim is to highlight what we now know as an extraordinarily rich category of material culture and demonstrate how it is increasingly contributing to our understanding of cognitive, technological, and social change. We argue that, despite this growing body of data, what are collectively and colloquially referred to simply as ‘bone tools’, remain largely ignored when grand narratives of human development are constructed. Consequently, our discipline is yet to fully benefit from their presence in the archaeological record, nor the increasingly sophisticated traceological analyses which have identified more tools, tool types, and activities than was previously thought possible. We aim to demonstrate that the corpus of bone technologies must be considered side-by-side with the mass of stone technologies if we are to better understand the technological and behavioral evolution of our species.

Introduction

The vital importance that hard animal materials played in the development of technology among ‘Stone Age’ societies was recognized very early in archaeological discourse. Lartet and Christy (1863) were among the first to note the sophistication of the bone and antler tools that were being recovered from the limestone matrices of the Dordogne Caves in France, and hypothesized that they must have had precursors in the Middle Paleolithic. Nevertheless, here and elsewhere, the focus of archaeologists in their reconstructions of past technological shifts remained on the more abundantly preserved stone artefacts. Almost a century later, the Australian anatomist working in South Africa, Raymond Dart, put forward the idea of an ‘osteodontokeratic culture' to explain what he thought was the preferential selection of certain skeletal elements, and their peculiar breakage patterns, by Australopithecines in the Earlier Stone Age deposits of the Makapans Valley (Dart 1957). Although this particular assemblage was later discredited when it was shown to be the result of taphonomic variables rather than intentional hominin action (Brain 1967), more recent discoveries in Africa, Asia, and Europe have shown that bone tools were as much a part of hominin technical and behavioral developments as their stone tools.

Bone tools also figure in additional, and often, profound understandings of human culture. Throughout the world, animals have served as pets, food, wealth, symbols of power, and of course, as raw material (Russell 2012; Overton and Hamilakis 2013). The fashioning of a tool from the skeletal remains of a once-living creature may have at times expressed a deep-seated spiritual link to the animal world to which humans belong, and simultaneously, from which they stand apart. This articulation between bone tool technology and human culture is addressed by ‘social zooarchaeology’, which explores questions pertaining to technical production strategies, specialization, transmission of technical knowledge, and the symbolic role of animals and animal products within past societies (see for example: Choyke 2013; Ingold 1988; Gates St-Pierre et al. 2018; Ryan and Crabtree 1995).

While bone tools are now acknowledged to be intimately entwined with the development of human cultures across the world, we would argue that bone tool data is yet to be fully appreciated in narratives surrounding the development of humanity. This situation is exemplified by broad scale reviews of human cognitive and technological evolution, which underline our increasingly complex understanding of the temporal and spatial appearance of different stone industries, but aggregate all bone artefacts into a single category, typically termed “bone tools” (e.g., Hussain and Will 2021; Mcbrearty and Brooks 2000; Scerri and Will 2023). This pooling of all bone tools into one catch-all box is a symptom of the lack of critical evaluation into the precise roles that these technologies played in our cognitive and cultural development. This lack of critical evaluation itself being a product of a general lack of awareness of just how diverse are the morphologies and functions of tools made on bone from their earliest appearance.

Below, we delve into the various functions that bone tools served in the Stone Age as brought to light through an increasing range of analytical methods, but most particularly, the increasingly common application of use-wear analysis. The term ‘Stone Age’ is used here interchangeably with Paleolithic and Mesolithic (ending c. 8,000 years ago), depending on the geographical context to which we are referring. We exclude from this review, the Neolithic and younger periods for the sake of concision and owing to the proliferation of bone tool forms and functions more readily recognized after this time and which would stymie any attempt at comprehensivity. In this paper, we describe only items made on bone—that is, excluding other osseous raw materials such as antler, tooth, and ivory. Although other hard animal materials had varying degrees of importance in Stone Age cultures, technologies made on bone are the first to appear in the archaeological record and bone as a raw material was available across all continents (Figure 1). Furthermore, attempting to weave in the differential selection and use of antler, tooth, and ivory to the already complex story as told solely by bone is an ongoing work which will require more than a single paper. For these reasons, we have chosen to confine ourselves here to items made on bone as a first step toward demonstrating the importance of meaningfully incorporating hard animal materials into grand narratives of human evolution.

We ask the question: what is the nature of the contribution of worked bone technology to our understanding of critical aspects of human evolution (sensu Hodder 1982)? We explore this issue in relation to the abilities and technologies that facilitated the trans-continental migrations of hominins, the expansion of economic and dietary resources, the expression of symbolic performances, and the refinement of other non-bone aspects of technology. In most cases, these technologies were expressed predominantly, if not exclusively, through the medium of bone. For example, improvements in stone tool knapping, such as soft hammer percussion and pressure flaking, arose concomitant with the adoption of osseous materials into the hominin toolkit. The ability of people to migrate into cooler climates was made possible by the adoption of well-fitted clothing and carrying baskets, both of which relied on bone implements as a critical component in their manufacture. Likewise, hominin dietary expansion to include aquatic resources was facilitated by tools that could not have been fashioned from stone. Symbolic aspects too, in the form of body adornments, musical instruments, and needles thin enough to pierce skin but malleable enough to carve a groove for holding ink, were largely expressed using bone as a raw material.

We hope to highlight the incredible range of activities for which bone was the preferred raw material among diverse hunter-gatherer societies, and how these focused studies not only enrich our understanding of the past, but are also a critical component of learning how we became human in the first place.

When is a ‘Bone Tool’ a ‘Bone Tool’?

Backwell and d’Errico (2014, pp. 950–951) define a ‘bone tool’ as “an implement that can achieve a task or modify or produce an item”. Curiously, they exclude from this definition “artefacts not used in functional activities”: things like ornaments, musical instruments, and notational devices. It is our contention, however, that all bone items serve a function, even if the function is ‘non-utilitarian’, ‘symbolic’, or purely for ‘aesthetic’ value. By ‘utilitarian’ we understand something that is designed to be useful or practical rather than attractive. Yet, as we show further on, something that is designed to be attractive still patently serves a function, i.e., to attract or to please. Furthermore, many utilitarian tools are aesthetically pleasing in their morphology, color, or finish—and as such—distinguishing the purely ‘utilitarian’ from the ‘non-utilitarian’ seems a false distinction.

Bone tools may also be divided into ‘formal’ and ‘informal’ categories. A ‘formal tool’ has been planned and shaped using techniques suited to bone, such as scraping, grinding, and grooving, but may also include tools purposefully shaped by knapping. An ‘informal tool’, on the other hand, is defined as a piece of bone that has been utilized opportunistically but not intentionally modified prior to use (Choyke 1997, p. 68; d’Errico et al. 2012a, pp. 2479, 2490; Ma and Doyon 2021, p. 2; Schibler 1981). Formal tools imply a certain degree of planning, standardization, and design and often reflect the economic or social importance of the task for which they were used, whereas informal tools more often reflect the immediate personal needs of the user (Backwell and d’Errico 2014; Choyke 1997, p. 68). Informal tools mostly arise out of the byproducts of food processing and often represent a significant component of the worked bone assemblage (e.g., Li and Shen 2010; Ma and Doyon 2021; Tartar 2012, p. 2352; Tejero et al. 2015, p. 94). Unfortunately, it is not always easy to recognize such minimally modified bone tools, leading to their under-representation in most bone tool studies and their resultant omission from our understanding of technological innovations (see Parfitt and Bello 2024).

Formal bone tools come in a wide variety of forms and were used for an enormous range of tasks. In the more recent periods that fall outside the temporal scope of our study, these range from hair combs (Ashby 2020; Walker 2007) to tattooing needles (Clark and Langley 2019; Gates St-Pierre 2018; Robitaille 2007); from ice-skates (MacGregor 1975; Semenov 1964, pp. 191–193; Thurber 2013) to musical flutes (Baron et al. 2022); from ophthalmic instruments (Van Beek and Van Beek 1990) to threshing sickles (Osipowicz et al. 2024; Spurrell 1892); from pottery scrapers (Buc and Loponte 2007; Legrand and Sidéra 2007) to appliances used to remove bark from trees (Bertolini and Hohenstein 2017)— and just about everything in between.

The complex relationship between the shape of a tool, from which its formal name is often derived, and its ultimate function has been highlighted by several authors (Backwell and d’Errico 2014; Bradfield 2016a; Gaudzinski 1999, p. 140; Langley 2023, pp. 42–43, 57; Webb and Allen 1990, pp. 77–78). Often, these names imply a specific function, and issues as diverse as subsistence economy and the evolution of technology are discussed with reference to these imputed functions, which may or may not bear any reality to the actual task for which a tool was used. For example, ‘awls’ are often implicitly understood to be piercing implements and are automatically associated with leather clothing manufacture, yet their shape does not preclude other functions, such as basketry, a task for which they have been shown to have been used in the European Mesolithic and through the deep past on the Australian continent (Langley 2023, pp. 74–87; van Gijn 2006). In other words, shape by itself may be a necessary but insufficient criterion to determine the precise function of an object. Indeed, several authors have noted the multiplicity of tasks for which a single bone tool morphotype is not only suited, but also often used (e.g., Gates St-Pierre 2007; Langley 2023; Mărgărit et al. 2022), creating a type of ‘Swiss army knife’ scenario, which is often under-appreciated by researchers. Indeed, studies have shown that in more recent periods, various technical and conceptual differences exist in bone tool manufacturing technology, even within the same morphotype, providing insights into various chronological, economic, and social aspects of past societies (Bradfield 2024; David 2013; Goutas and Tejero 2016).

Resource Gathering and Processing Tools

We begin our review of bone technologies with those items used to gather and process foods and for other subsistence activities. Perhaps not surprisingly, it is within this realm that the earliest examples of bone tools have been identified, stretching back beyond two million years. Below, we group together tools with similar functions as challenges remain in the conclusive identification of specific tasks which share commonalities in use trace production. Nevertheless, even with our current level of traceological (and typological) capability the range of identified tools is broad, as will become evident below.

Subterranean Harvesters and Bark Removers

The earliest evidence that we have for the use of bone as a tool predates the emergence of our species by a considerable margin. Beginning some 2.3 million years ago, long bone shafts were being fashioned into crude digging implements in southern Africa (Figure 2F; Backwell and d’Errico 2001; d’Errico and Backwell 2003; Hanon et al. 2021; Stammers et al. 2018). To date, more than a hundred bone tools, dated to between 2.3 and 0.6 million years ago, and associated with the remains of archaic Homo and Australopithecus robustus, have been recovered from various karstic sites in the Cradle of Humankind World Heritage Site, an area of some 470 km2. Microwear evidence suggests that these tools were used to forage in sediment, perhaps to extract termites from their mounds or to harvest tubers (Backwell and d’Errico 2001, 2003; Hanon et al. 2021; Stammers et al. 2018). The potential role of taphonomic variables in the creation of these artefacts has been tentatively raised (Kuman 2005), but experimental simulations have ruled out the possibility that the microwear present on the Cradle bones could have resulted from natural sediment abrasion processes (Senyane et al. 2023). Additionally, some of the bones purportedly show signs of intentional shaping, in the form of grinding, prior to use (Backwell and d’Errico 2005, 2009; Stammers et al. 2018). Although it is not known which of the two hominin species used these tools, the fact that some appear to have been intentionally manufactured implies that the makers had a clear understanding of the relationship between the shape of the tools and how they were intended to be used (d’Errico 2003).

Bones continued to be used as digging implements in the African Middle Stone Age but with a slight alteration in their form. Double-beveled or wedge-shaped tools are found in 80,000–60,000-year-old deposits at Sibudu, South Africa. Comparative microwear analysis reveals that these tools most likely served to debark trees and dig in humus-rich soils, perhaps to forage for tubers (d’Errico et al. 2022). These tools are thought to represent a regional technological tradition that lasted for at least 20,000 years. Given the dearth of focused bone tool research at other sites, however, it remains possible that additional examples may yet be recognized.

The Sibudu bone wedges are on average much smaller than the later occurrences of bone mattocks that appear in the European Mesolithic and which are also interpreted either as digging implements (Gramsch 1973; Kufel and Diakowski 2008; Semenov 1964, p. 6) or tools used to remove bark from trees and otherwise perform wood-working tasks (Orłowska and Osipowicz 2017; van Gijn 2006). Informal bone tools, made from fragments of long bone diaphyses, are identified as bark removal implements from as early as the Aurignacian period in Europe, where their informal nature has been used to argue for a more gradual shift from Middle to Upper Paleolithic technology than is apparent in the lithic record (Tartar 2012). There have also been suggestions that this tool may stretch back into Neanderthal Middle Paleolithic contexts (Sandgathe and Hayden 2003). Similarly shaped worked bones occur at several sites in the Beringian refugium during the terminal Pleistocene migration period (Bonnichsen 1979), but we are not aware of any use-wear analysis that has been undertaken to confirm the function of these artefacts. As such, more detailed work is required in a number of regions and on assemblages from a range of time periods in order to confirm suspected bone harvesting tools or identify new examples.

Butchering and Cutting

Twenty-seven knapped long bones have recently been reported from c. 1.5-million-year-old deposits at Olduvai Gorge and have been interpreted as butchering tools (la Torre et al. 2025). The earliest bone handaxe appears at Konso in Ethiopia and was made on a 1.4-million-year-old hippopotamus femur. Use-wear analysis conducted on this tool found that one side was used to cut or saw in a longitudinal motion, with the opposite side probably being held in the hand (Figure 2G; Sano et al. 2020). Similar bone handaxes also occur at numerous sites throughout the Middle to Late Pleistocene. Examples have been found in Italy (Boschian and Saccá 2015; Peretto et al. 1997, p. 613; Segre and Ascenzi 1984, p. 232; Segre et al. 1987), Germany (Brühl 2003, p. 52; Schwarcz et al. 1988), Hungary (Kretzoi and Dobosi 1990), and the Levant (Rabinovich et al. 2012; Zutovski and Barkai 2016), all dating from about 500,000 to 300,000 years ago. A microwear study of several of these bone handaxes and associated faunal material concluded that the handaxes were used for butchery (Bello et al. 2009).

These bifaces are in many cases made from bones of very large mammals, the marrow from which was an important component of the diet of early hominins (Domínguez-Rodrigo et al. 2012; Radmilli and Boschian 1996). Studies of their chaîne opératoire suggest that whole bones were knapped specifically with the aim of producing the bifaces rather than for marrow extraction (Sano et al. 2020; Zutovski and Barkai 2016). It is particularly interesting to note that the production of Acheulian bifaces in bone is additional to those made in stone and therefore not related to a scarcity of knappable stone, which is often put forward as a reason for bone raw material selection. Owing to the multiple hominin species known to be in the wider region at this phase of the Lower Paleolithic, it is not currently known which species was responsible for these osseous tools, but the identification of flaked bone tools at this early period of human evolution demonstrates the continued use of osseous raw materials since early in our technological development.

Later manifestations of bone cutting tools appear as spatulate-form blades at Dar es-Solton I Cave in Morocco at 90,000 years ago (Bouzouggar et al. 2018). Bone tools of similar morphology had earlier been found in slightly older deposits at El Mnasra (El Hajraoui 1993, pp. 107–109; El Hajraoui and Debénath 2012), but, owing to the lack of use-wear analysis, these tools have not featured in discussions of Aterian technology. The use-wear results from Dar es-Solton I Cave, viewed in conjunction with similarly shaped bone tools from other sites, highlights the strong probability that many more such tools exist that are currently hidden behind a nebulous and unhelpful morphological nomenclature, such as ‘wedges’ and ‘spatulas’.

In the Late Pleistocene of North America, bone rods and wedges display similar microwear that indicates their use in butchery activities, both for slicing flesh and joint dismemberment (Fisher 1984; Fisher et al. 1994; Saunders and Daeschler 1994; Shipman et al. 1984). Bone knives and knife handles are replaced by antler after the Late Paleoindian Period until the end of the Late Archaic period when bone is again adopted for this purpose (Byrd 2011). Bone knives and knife handles make an appearance at the start of the Holocene in China (Zhang et al. 2018, p. 87) and North Africa (Petrullo and Barich 2021) but do not appear to have enjoyed a long popularity. The brief florescence of bone knives is most likely due to bone being ill-suited to retaining a sharp cutting edge. Indeed, as Zutovski and Barkai (2016) speculated with regards to the Lower Paleolithic bone handaxes, their ill-suitedness for purpose, coupled with the small scale of their production and the fact that they are predominantly made from the bones of very large mammals, such as elephant and mammoth, may suggest a symbolic function for these artefacts.

Hunting and Fishing

Possibly the oldest bone hunting weapon is believed to be a poorly preserved rib fragment from an Acheulean context associated with Homo erectus at Olduvai Gorge. This specimen has what appears to be three uniserial barbs that purportedly show signs of anthropogenic scraping (Pante et al. 2020, pp. 9–10). The specimen is, however, very poorly preserved and the technology imputed suspiciously old. A more accepted candidate for the oldest barbed bone weapon dates to c. 90,000 years ago and comes from Katanda (Democratic Republic of the Congo), a site which also has the oldest known hafted bone points (Figure 3B; Brooks et al. 1995, 2006; Feathers and Migliorini 2001; Yellen 1998; Yellen et al. 1995).

After this precocious appearance of the Katanda barbed technology, barbed points do not reappear in sub-Saharan Africa until c. 20,000 years ago at Ishango (also in the Democratic Republic of the Congo) (Brooks and Smith 1987; de Heinzelin 1962), before becoming a common occurrence in Later Stone Age sites throughout the region, where they occur as miniaturized versions of their older counterparts (e.g., Barthelme 1977, pp. 35–37, 1985; Monod and Mauny 1957; Petit-Marie et al. 1983, pp. 119, 121; Phillipson 1977, pp. 20–25; Robbins 1974; Wendt 1966, pp. 3, 8–11; Yellen 1998). The southernmost African barbed bone points have been recovered from White Paintings Rock Shelter (Botswana), with the oldest example at this site perhaps dating to the Late Pleistocene, and the youngest overlying a charcoal date of 2260 years BP (Robbins et al. 1994; Figure 3F).

Interestingly, barbed bone points have not been recovered from either Middle Stone Age or Later Stone Age deposits in other southern African territories, though a single fragmentary unilaterally barbed bone point associated with an Iberomaurusian industry (bracketed by radiocarbon dates of 10,800 and 12,070 years ago) has been found at Taforalt, Morocco (Camps 1974, pp. 73–74). Given the similarities of this particular artefact to those made and utilized by contemporaneous peoples across the Strait of Gibraltar (Villaverde et al. 2016), some researchers have speculated on the possibility that Taforalt barbed bone was inspired by the neighboring Magdalenian technology (Otte 1997; Straus 2001), or indeed, vice versa.

In Europe, barbed points manufactured from both terrestrial and marine bone are rare in comparison to those made from antler. For the larger European corpus of osseous (antler, bone, and ivory) barbed points, the earliest well-dated (including direct dates on artefacts) examples come from Fontalès, d’Espalunge, Isturitz, and Tito Bustillo—all of which date to around 16,000–15,500 years ago (Pétillon et al. 2015; Szmidt et al. 2010; Tisnerat-Laborde et al. 1997), and continue to the end of the Late Magdalenian (c. 12,200 years ago) before being replaced by Azilian (an Epipaleolithic culture) barbed points in these same regions. Many of these studies do not, unfortunately, distinguish between those made from bone and those of antler, and as such we can only provide a broad-brush overview of osseous points in total. By the Mesolithic period, unilateral barbed bone points are a common feature in northern Europe from Doggerland in the North Sea to Estonia on the Baltic (Amkreutz and Spithoven 2019; David 2007; Kozłowski 1969; Orłowska and Osipowicz 2018; Osipowicz 2016). The dimensional variability evident within and between assemblages in these periods suggests that the barbed points were perhaps used to signal group identity, and that they may have been used to hunt both aquatic and terrestrial resources, although the exact method of deployment is still debated (Amkreutz and Spithoven 2019, p. 396; Bahn 1983, p. 184; Brun 1867, p. 18; Langley 2019; Pétillon 2008, 2009; Pokines and Krupa 1997; Weniger 2000).

Moving to the east, the oldest examples of barbed bone points outside of Africa have been found in 30,000–23,000-year-old deposits in Xiaogushan and 23,000- to 18,000-year-old deposits at Ma’anshan Cave, China. The Xiaogushan artefact is a bilaterally barbed point made on artiodactyla bone (Huang et al. 1986), while both uni- and bilaterally barbed types appear to be present at Ma’anshan Cave (Zhang et al. 2016, p. 61).

Barbed bone points are relatively rare in Western Asia, first appearing in the Levant during the Natufian period (c. 15,000–12,000 years ago), with the largest sample (consisting of only seven artefacts) recovered from Kebara Cave (Israel) dating to around 11,000 years ago (Yellen 1998, pp. 180, 185). Here, the barbed points are traditionally associated with fishing, possibly owing to the appearance of other bone fishing technology in this context (bipoints, fishhooks, and gorges) (Campana 1991; Henry 1989, p. 197; Stordeur 1991), though Henry (1989, p. 197) suggests they could have been utilized in hunting terrestrial prey.

Unbarbed projectile points demonstrate both greater antiquity and spatial distribution. In Africa, early examples dated by optically stimulated luminescence (OSL) to between c. 107,000 and 106,000 years ago have been found at El Mnasara and Katanda (El Hajraoui and Debénath 2012; Jacobs et al. 2012). These are joined by small assemblages from the Still Bay layers of Blombos Cave dated to 75,000 years ago (d’Errico and Henshilwood 2007), as well as the pre-Still Bay layers at Sibudu Cave dated to c. 72,000 years ago (Backwell and d’Errico 2016; d’Errico et al. 2012a; Jacobs et al. 2008a, b). Older bone points of similar morphology have been found at, for example, Broken Hill in Zambia, dated to between 300,000 and 140,000 years ago (Barham et al. 2002), but no functional studies have yet been undertaken. Although the robusticity of the Blombos bone points was initially used to argue for their use as spearheads (d'Errico and Henshilwood 2007; Backwell and d’Errico 2016), subsequent studies of their tip cross-sectional areas indicate that they nevertheless fall within the range of ethnographic arrowheads (Lombard 2020). More convincing examples of bow-and-arrow technology come from > 60,000-year-old deposits at two other South African sites, namely Sibudu and Klasies River Main site (Figure 3F, G; Backwell et al. 2008, 2018; Bradfield et al. 2020; Lombard 2011, 2020; Lombard and Phillipson 2010). The Klasies River Main sites bone point is thought to have been used with the accompaniment of poison and could signal the genesis of what would become a well-established technological accompaniment to hunting (Bradfield et al. 2020, 2024; Chaboo et al. 2019). Bone points disappear from the archaeological record after the Howiesons Poort, reappearing only 20,000 years later at sites such as White Paintings Rock Shelter in Botswana (Robbins et al. 2012).

Outside of Africa, bone points are first found associated with Neanderthals. The oldest of these comes from a Middle Paleolithic layer dated to between 80,000 and 70,000 years old at Mezmaiskaya Cave in the Caucasus. This particular specimen has recently been interpreted as an arrowhead on the basis of impact fracture damage and an associated bituminous residue (Golovanova et al. 2025). Bow-and-arrow technology at this date is precociously old for the region and, if this interpretation is correct, would imply a sophisticated techno-behavior not previously attributed to Neanderthals (but see Zilhão et al. 2010 for evidence of the symbolic use of marine shells and pigments by Iberian Neandertals at this time). In Europe, Mateo-Lomba et al. (2024) have described a knapped bone spear point coming from the c. 50,000-year-old Neanderthal-associated layers of Abric Romaní, Spain. These two recent discoveries beg the question whether more such points will be uncovered in the future as greater focus is placed on the worked bone component of these early sites. Certainly, this work demonstrates the ability of interdisciplinary analysis to identify new forms of bone tools.

Unbarbed points—mostly in antler—but some in bone are well-represented throughout Western and Central Europe, becoming more numerous and diverse in design throughout the European Upper Paleolithic, prompting Straus (1993, p. 83) to dub these artefacts “the most dynamic component of the Upper Paleolithic technologies”. Aurignacian (starting around 43,000 years ago; the chronology of the Aurignacian is highly contested: see Zilhão and d’Errico 1999; Higham et al. 2012) hunting kits contained split-based points and simple-based points (Karavanić 2016; Tejero 2016). Although normally associated with Neanderthals, Aurignacian sites in Slovenia, such as Potočka zijalka where bone points have been found dating to 35,000 years ago, demonstrate a greater Homo sapiens cultural affiliation (Moreau et al. 2015; Odar 2011). Gravettian (c. 29,000–22,000 years ago) assemblages comprise simple-based points, beveled-based points, Isturitz points, and simple-based points with mesial incisions (Goutas 2016). Later still, Magdalenian (21,000–14,000 years ago) kits exhibit a huge range of osseous and composite osseous-lithic types (Chauviére 2016; Langley et al. 2016a; Villaverde et al. 2016), while extensive Mesolithic bone-lithic composite assemblages are described for some regions, such as for Ivanovskoye 7 in Russia (Zhilin 2017). Again, while antler dominates these industries, bone examples are present but lack of distinction between these two materials inhibits a more detailed discussion of these pieces.

Unbarbed points of various sizes and proximal (hafting) morphologies are also found in South Asia (Anderson 1990, p. 32; Perera et al. 2016), Island Southeast Asia (Aplin et al. 2016), Australia (Allen et al. 2016b, a), and North America (O’Brien et al. 2016). The attributes of each weapon tip were dictated by the raw materials available for point manufacture, the target fauna, the landscape in which the hunting occurred, and the community of practice in which the weapon was produced. The oldest example of bone points associated with bow-and-arrow technology outside of Africa comes from 48,000-year-old deposits at the site of Fa-Hien Lena in Sri Lanka (Langley et al. 2020), while small bone bipoints thought to have been used as fishing gorges were found in 30,000-year-old levels at Bubong I, Occidental Mindoro, Philippines (Boulanger et al. 2023, p. 3; Pawlik et al. 2015). At Niah Caves (Sarawak), several examples of small bone bipoints dating to the Terminal Pleistocene/Early Holocene were found to retain evidence for hafting in the form of mastics and fibers (Figure 3A; Barton et al. 2009; Rabett 2005; Rabett et al. 2013). In neighboring Timor-Leste, a pointed bone object with several denticulations on its left and right edges dating to about 34,000 years ago was recovered from Matja Kuru 2 (Figure 3C; O’Connor et al. 2014). The excavators of this artefact suggest that the denticulations were to aid in the hafting of the object, though other interpretations remain possible owing to the fragmentary state of the piece. Despite this ambiguity in function, however, the uniqueness of this find provides a glimpse into the complexity of Pleistocene-aged bone technology that was enacted in this region once considered a cultural back-water.

In Europe, the identification of numerous foreshafts (and points) made from cetacean bone dating to the Middle to Late Magdalenian (c. 17,500–15,000 years ago) has provided insight into the opportunistic use of beached resources (no evidence for hunting of live whales during this period has been found). Analysis of the spatial distribution of these artefacts allowed Pétillon (2013) to conclude that the bone was exclusively of Atlantic origin, with objects made from this material being transported along the Pyrenees up to the central part of the range some 350 km away, and east along the Cantabrian coast (Lefebvre et al. 2021; McGrath et al. 2025). Similarly, the discovery of a sole foreshaft in cetacean bone from the Late Magdalenian open-air site of Andernach-Martinsberg (Central German Rhineland) indicated that these artefacts were sometimes transported over significantly longer distances—in this case, more than 1000 km (Langley and Street 2013).

Despite the interest in the time depth of aquatic resource exploitation, the identification of Pleistocene fishing technology used across space and time has remained largely elusive. The oldest proposed method is line-fishing. Small bone bipoints recovered from various Late Pleistocene contexts across the globe have been interpreted as having been part of composite fishing technology, either as gorges (‘gorge’ meaning throat or gullet) or as parts of multi-component hooks (Allen et al. 2016b, a, p. 214; Bradfield 2019; Évora 2016; Goutas 2016; Perera et al. 2016; Turville-Petre 1932, pp. 272, 276). Such bone bipoints have been recovered from three sites along the South African coast, all dating between 12,000 and 8000 years ago (Figure 3D; Klein 1974, pp. 53–59; Schweitzer and Wilson 1978, p. 138). Fragments of similar-looking artefacts have been found at Die Kelders, Smitswinkelbaai, Elands Bay, Nelson Bay, and Byneskranskop but not all of these artefacts can be confidently attributed to the same artefact category owing to their sometimes incomplete and fragmentary condition (Bradfield 2019). In Western Europe, ‘gorges’, ‘darts’, or ‘hameçon droits’ are described for a number of Magdalenian (21,000–14,000 years ago) contexts and similarly attributed to fishing or birding technologies (e.g., Bellier and Cattelain 1998; Langley et al. 2016a, pp. 145, 148; Parent 1980). In Australia, small bone bipoints, some flaked and some ground into shape, and which have been identified based on morphology, use-wear, and residues as having tipped multi-pronged fishing spears have also been reported. While most specimens date to the Mid-to-Late Holocene (Langley et al. 2021b, 2023), an example on bird bone dating to c. 42,000 years ago was found at the Mimbi site of Riwi in the south-central Kimberley, hinting at earlier traditions (Langley et al. 2021a, p. 680).

Clearly identifiable bone fishhooks don’t appear in the archaeological record till the Terminal Pleistocene, with the earliest reported examples coming from Epipaleolithic sites dated to after c. 15,000 years ago in the Levant (Pedergnana et al. 2021; Turville-Petre 1932, p. 272, 276) and European Final Paleolithic contexts including examples from the sites of Klein Lieskow, Germany (Gramsch et al. 2013, p. 2461; Pasda 2001); Grotte du Bois-Ragot and Pont d’Ambon, France (Chollet et al. 1976; Cleyet-Merle 1990); and Gratkorn, Austria (Pittioni 1954). These hooks often appear in complex rotating or jabbing forms with projecting barbs, indicating that these artefacts are already the product of extensive experimentation and design. It should be noted that older examples of jabbing and rotating fishhooks have been found in marine shell in the Pacific (Fujita et al. 2016; O’Connor et al. 2011), and interestingly, bone fishhooks do not appear in Africa until well into the Holocene (Bradfield and Choyke 2016).

The final form of hunting equipment to be described are boomerangs or throwing sticks. One such item has been reported thus far, a fragment of a boomerang made on mammoth bone recovered from an Upper Paleolithic context at Stillfried (Austria), though its exact cultural affiliation remains unknown (Kriegler 1962). These throwing weapons are more difficult to identify as their method of use does not ordinarily produce the high-fricative contact that facilitates the identification by use-wear of other projectiles (but see Langley et al. 2016b). As such, it may be that bone throwing weapons are underrepresented.

Tool-Making Tools

Around the time that sections of long bone were being used as digging tools in southern Africa, they were also being selected and utilized for the working of stone. As such, bone tools, whose primary purpose was to work other raw materials to create pieces of material culture, enjoy a similar antiquity to subsistence-getting items. We begin again with the oldest examples and group together potentially similar technologies.

Anvils, Soft Hammers, and Pressure Flakers

At Olduvai Gorge in present-day Tanzania, fossil bones have been found in almost two-million-year-old deposits with percussion damage suggestive of use as hammers or anvils (Backwell and d’Errico 2004, 2014; Pante et al. 2020). This use-damage is found primarily on the femoral condyles, distal humeri, astragali, and patellae of large animals (Figure 2A-C). Although some of this battering is superficially indistinguishable from that stemming from marrow processing, the remains of these particular animals are otherwise rare in Olduvai assemblages, indicating deliberate targeting for tool manufacture. The rarity of these artefacts points to the episodic, and perhaps opportunistic, nature of bone tool use by early Homo at this period. In their recent reanalysis of some of the modified Olduvai bones described by Mary Leakey (1994), Pante and colleagues (2020) note the similarity of percussion marks found on a distal hippopotamus humerus to those produced on soft hammers used to make stone tools. The use of soft hammers in stone tool reduction is indeed seen in the Mode 2 Acheulian techno-complex (~1.76 to 1.5 million years ago), although the use of a bone hammer is not an exclusively necessary component as other ‘soft’ mediums such as wood, horn or antler were available (Clément 2022).

Early examples of bone retouchers are first seen outside of Africa about half a million years ago at sites like Marathousa in Greece (Tourloukis et al. 2018, pp. 57–59) and Boxglove and Clacton-on-sea in the United Kingdom (Parfitt and Bello 2024; Parfitt et al. 2022; Stout et al. 2014, pp. 580–581). At these sites, metatarsals and tibiae from medium- to large-sized bovids, apparently broken for non-nutritional purposes, display diagnostic impact marks suggesting their use in stone knapping. The association of soft hammer percussors with Mode 1 lithic technology at these sites blurs one of the main distinctions between Modes 1 and 2 technologies, namely, the use of soft hammer percussion. Bone retouchers and hammers appear at several European and Levantine sites in the 500,000 to 300,000 BP period. In the famous spear horizon at Schöningen, Germany, the absence of stone hammers at this period indicates that bone may have completely substituted for this task. Altogether 88 bone retouchers and anvils were recovered from Schöningen, all indicating a short use-life, and therefore that they were perhaps utilized as informal tools (Hutson et al. 2018a; Van Kolfschoten et al. 2015). On the contrary, at Qesem Cave in Israel and Bolomor Cave in Spain, evidence suggests intentional shaping prior to use, although suitability of shape does seem to be the determining factor in the selection of these bone retouchers (Blasco et al. 2013; Rosell et al. 2018; Figure 2E). In many cases, the bone tools had previously been dismissed by archaeologists as the result of natural damage (perhaps in part owing to Brain’s and other taphonomists’ cautioning against hasty anthropogenic attributions) and many more probably remain unrecognized in faunal assemblages (see Hutson et al. 2018b; Parfitt and Bello 2024, p. 8). The benefits of focused microwear analysis are thus highlighted in just this single functional category.

Bone hammers and pressure flakers persist into the Middle Paleolithic in Europe. Although their presence is more often inferred from lithic studies, bone artefacts have been found at numerous Middle (Neanderthal), transitional (e.g., Uluzzian, Châtelperonian), and Upper (Homo sapiens) Paleolithic contexts stretching from the western edge of Europe to Siberia (e.g., Arrighi et al. 2020, pp. 171–175; Baumann et al. 2020, 2023; Bello et al. 2021; d’Errico and Backwell 2007; Parfitt and Bello 2024; Semenov 1964, p. 177; Toniato et al. 2018). Worthy of specific mention are the Italian Late Mousterian sites, which are particularly rich in bone retouchers. These retouchers are usually produced from unmodified diaphysis fragments and extend into the Proto-Aurignacian deposits in this region (Arrighi et al. 2020; Jéquier et al. 2018; Martellotta et al. 2020).

At the Mousterian site of La Quina in France, three human cranial bones display percussion damage, similar to that found on several long bone shaft fragments at the site, suggesting their use as retouchers. Scrape marks indicate that the bones were prepared prior to use and therefore represent formal tools (Verna and d’Errico 2011). These three cranial fragments remain some of the earliest evidence for the use of human bone for tools, opening lines of enquiry about the possible antiquity of what is known to be socially and/or spiritually charged material in the ethnohistoric present (e.g., Langley 2023, pp. 144–150). At the Mousterian site of Troisième Caverne in Belgium, Neanderthal bones display similar percussion damage as well as evidence of butchery (Rougier et al. 2016), with similar finds also reported at the French sites of Les Pradelle and Tourtoirac (Crevecoeur et al. 2024; Mussini 2011) as well as at Krapina in Croatia (Patou-Mathis 1997). Quite apart from what these artefacts tell us about Neanderthal technology they are also informative about aspects of Neanderthal mortuary practices.

Bone retouchers and soft hammer percussors are also found throughout the African Middle Stone Age, from Sibudu in South Africa (d’Errico et al. 2012a; Henshilwood et al. 2001) to Taforalt, El Harhoura 2, and Contrebandiers Cave in Morocco (Turner et al. 2020). In China, bone retouchers and pressure flakers made from cervid metapodials and limb bone fragments from large- to medium-size mammals appear in the pre-100,000-year levels at the Lingjing open-air site in Henan Province (Doyon et al. 2018, 2019; Figure 2D). Here, both formal and informal bone retouchers were noted, with informal retouchers made from appropriate bone flakes arising from marrow extraction. Formal retouchers, however, were made from fashioning pieces of weathered bone into suitable splinters and appear to have been used for much longer duration than the informal examples (Doyon et al. 2019). Interesting to note is that the preferential selection of the metapodials may have been because of its natural ergonomic prehensility, and we must therefore consider if such careful selection constitutes an informal or formal tool category. Noted variations in regional and temporal manufacturing practices may reflect social boundaries (Ma and Doyon 2021), an aspect which will unfold as research progresses in this region.

Evidence of bone pressure flakers in the Early Paleoindian period (c. 13,300–11,900 cal. BP) of North America appears through direct and indirect evidence in the form of pressure-flaked stone tools and associated bone ‘rods’, which have been interpreted as handles of retouchers (Graf and Buvit 2017; Wilke et al. 1991), though there is a range of interpretations of these rods (see O’Brien et al. 2016 for discussion and see below). We are not aware of any direct use trace evidence linking these or any other bone artefacts to lithic reduction during the Late Pleistocene in North America.

On the Australian continent, a possible percussor made on a flaked macropod tibia was found dating to around 35,000 years ago at Riwi in the Kimberley (Langley et al. 2021a, pp. 679–680), and it is possible that other similar informal bone tools have been missed or are yet to be found in the faunal assemblages that survive to discovery.

Finally, the practice of hafting bone punches and pressure flakers does not appear until the start of the Holocene, but not in all regions (i.e., in Australia where they remain unhafted). Sites with bone retouchers proliferate, as does their variety, during the past 10,000 years (David and Sørensen 2016; Langley 2023, pp. 135–136; O’Brien et al. 2016, p. 231; Zhang et al. 2018, p. 84).

Hide-Working and Garment-Making

The appearance of clothing lice (Pediculus humanus humanus) has been traced back using genetic analysis as far as 170,000–80,000 years ago, indicating humans have been wearing clothing for at least this long (Boyd et al. 2017; Kittler et al. 2003; Toups et al. 2011). The ability to clothe oneself and make leather bags or pouches and sandals likely facilitated the long-distance movement of people into colder climates (d’Errico et al. 2018; Doyon 2019; Hallett et al. 2021). Body coverings likely also afforded some protection against insect attacks and associated tropical diseases (Langley et al. 2020). Garment manufacture therefore signals an evolutionary advancement of our species, much like the invention of the first projectile weapons. Three types of bone tool are commonly associated with clothing manufacture—and more specifically—with working hides: lissoirs, awls, and needles.

The lissoir (also called “smoothers” or “burnishers”) is used to produce supple and impermeable hides and furs, and are most often made on the rib bones of ungulates. Possible examples that conform to the general shape of a lissoir have been found in Lower Paleolithic contexts in Europe, including at Castel di Guido (Italy) dated to c. 395,000 years ago (Villa et al. 2021) and from c. 350,000-year-old levels at Schöningen, Germany (Julien et al. 2015). The earliest microwear-supported examples, however, are from 120,000–90,000-year-old deposits at Contrebandiers Cave in Morocco associated with Homo sapiens (Figure 4A; Hallett et al. 2021) and from Neanderthal contexts associated with Mousterian of Acheulian Tradition (MTA) at Pech-de-l’Aze I (c. 51,000 years old) and Abri Peyrony (47,000–41,000 years ago) in the Dordogne, southwest France (Figure 4B; Soressi et al. 2013). These four artefacts are made on rib fragments of medium-size ungulates (red deer or reindeer) and display use-wear consistent with ethnographically known hide-working implements. Other examples dated to c. 42,000–40,000 years ago have been reported from the Mousterian levels of Abri Lartet in France (Baumann et al. 2022) and from later Châtelperronian contexts at other sites (d’Errico et al. 1998b, S4-S5).

Once Homo sapiens arrive in Europe, we also find these tools in Proto-Aurignacian (Julien et al. 2002) and Aurignacian deposits (Leroy-Prost 1975, 1979; Moreau et al. 2015), as well as in later Upper Paleolithic techno-complexes (Averbouh and Buisson 2004; Martisius et al. 2022) before becoming common in the Holocene. In Africa, three possible examples of this tool have been found at Sibudu Cave in Howiesons Poort and post-Howiesons Poort levels (Backwell et al. 2008; d’Errico et al. 2012a).

The bone tool most commonly associated with working hides is the ‘borer’ or ‘awl’. Awls are described as tools made on bone fragments whose active (distal) end is slightly worked by scraping or abrasion and are used to perforate soft materials (Camps-Fabrer 1990). The problem with identifying these tools, is that in highly fragmented assemblages where only the pointed tip is preserved, they can easily be mistaken for other pointed artefact forms, such as projectile points, (see Langley 2023, pp. 74–87 for discussion in the Australian context, but which is globally relevant).

Bone awls are only rarely identified in the African Middle Stone Age and from Lower and Middle Paleolithic contexts in Eurasia (Bordes 1984, pp. 43; Gaudzinski 1999; Howell and Freeman 1983). In Africa, only two Middle Stone Age sites, Blombos Cave (c. 76,000–71,000 years ago) and Sibudu (c. 65,000–61,000 years ago), have yielded bone awls suitable for piercing skins and which exhibit appropriate use-wear (Backwell et al. 2008; d’Errico et al. 2012a, b, c; Henshilwood et al. 2001). Bone awls appear in younger contexts at Peers, Klasies, Sibudu, and Border Cave (Backwell et al. 2008).

In Asia, the earliest hide-piercing tools come from Lingjing, Henan Province, China, and are dated to c. 100,000–80,000 years ago (Li and Shen 2010). These tools are mostly informal, minimally modified shaft fragments that nevertheless retain use-wear indicative of hide scraping and perforating.

Formal bone awls likely used to pierce hides have been recovered from Neanderthal-associated Mousterian and Châtelperronian contexts, such as at Grotte du Renne, Arcy-sur-Cure, France, which dates to 45,000–42,000 years ago (d’Errico et al. 2003). The authors of this study suggest that it is likely that the thinnest awls found in this context were used to pierce furs, bird hides, or even less strong materials such as intestines (d’Errico et al. 2003, p. 265). Bone awls are also found in the so-called ‘transitional techno-complexes’ such as the Uluzzian of southern Italy (Arrighi et al. 2020; d’Errico et al. 1998b; Vincent 1993) and from the Initial Upper Paleolithic level of Denisova Cave (Russia), dated to between 48,000 and 37,000 years ago (Derevianko 2010). After c. 42,000 years ago, bone awls become a pervasive feature of the Eurasian Upper Paleolithic toolkit (Figure 4C; Akhmetgaleeva 2017; Bietti and Negrino 2008; Bodu and Mevel 2008, pp. 518–519; Camps-Fabrer et al. 1990; Güleç et al. 2002; Gurioli et al. 2011; Hoffecker 2005, pp. 188, 190; Langlais et al. 2010; Yanevich 2014, p. 558). In the Levant also, bone awls have been found in Ahmarian (c. 41,000–33,000 BP) and Levantine Aurignacian (c. 38,000–34,000 BP) contexts (Belfer-Cohen and Bar-Yosef 1981, pp. 30–32; Coinman 1996; Gilead 1991, pp. 138–139; Newcomer and Watson 1984; Tartar 2009; Tejero 2013; Tejero et al. 2015).

The last type of hide-working bone tool that we will discuss here is the needle. The invention of eyed bone needles is thought to be directly related to the creation of closer-fitting sewn clothing, a technological development critical to the ability of humans to move into higher latitudes. Eyed bone needles are best represented in the European Upper Paleolithic, with the earliest clear examples identified at well-preserved Russian Early Upper Paleolithic sites, including Denisova Cave dating somewhere between 50,000 and 11,000 years ago (Derevianko et al. 2016), Kostenki–Borshchevo, dating to c. 40,000–30,000 years ago (Hoffecker et al. 2008), Mezmaiskaya Cave within layers dated to c. 33,000–28,000 years ago (Golovanova et al. 2010a, 2010b), and Strashnaya Cave in the Altai dating to c. 44,000–19,000 years ago (Shalagina et al. 2018). Studies of some of the Paleolithic needles by Stettler (1998) found a decrease in the diameter of needle eyes between the Solutrean (c. 21,000–18,000 years ago) and the Magdalenian (c. 18,000–12,000 years ago), with greater standardization of needle eyes in the Later Magdalenian than the Early Magdalenian. This decrease and then standardization of the needle eye diameter is likely owing to changes in what thread was being used (from larger leather, plant fiber, or sinew strands), increasing familiarity and skill with this technology, and possibly also new forms of sewn material culture being experimented with or innovated (see Gilligan et al. 2024 for discussion).

Moving east into Asia, the oldest eyed boned needles in China are currently from Xiaogushan, a Late Paleolithic site dating to 30,000–20,000 years ago (Figure 4D; Huang and Fu 2009, p. 79; Norton and Jin 2009, 254; Zhang et al. 2010). Paleolithic eyed bone needles are also known from Xiaogushan, Zhoukoudian Upper Cave, Shuidonggou, Xianrendong, and Shizitan, all dating between 30,000 and 11,000 years ago (Wang et al. 2020). The morphometric differences in bone needles between those from Siberia and those from northern China are thought to signal independent invention in each region (d’Errico et al. 2018; Doyon 2019). Moving east again into North America, examples dating back to c. 13,000 years ago have been identified at a number of sites located in Alaska, Washington, Idaho, Nevada, Wyoming, Colorado, Texas, Nebraska, and Missouri (Figure 4E; Osborn 2014; Lyman 2015). The high-quality workmanship and narrow morphometric range of Paleoindian needles is thought to reflect a mastery of bone tool production that had not been attained prior to the crossing of the Bering Strait land bridge (d’Errico et al. 2018).

After c. 30,000 years ago, eyed and uneyed bone needles appear regularly in the archaeological record, having been recovered from about 256 sites across Eurasia and some 15 sites in North America alone (Arrighi et al. 2020; d’Errico et al. 2018; Soffer et al. 2001; Stone 2011; Stordeur-Yedid 1979).

Weaving Tools

Following Adovasio (2010, p. 1, 2021, p. 120), we here use the term ‘basketry’ to refer to a class of textile which is woven by hand with frame or loom and which encompasses not just containers, but also mats, bags, cradles, fish traps, and other forms. We know that basketry technology is at least 27,000 to 29,000 years old thanks to fired clay impressions found in several Pavlovian sites in Moravia (Czech Republic) (Adovasio et al. 1996; Soffer et al. 2000, 2001). The earliest possible bone points linked to weaving, however, are not identified until 10,000 years later. Desmond (2022) identified possible bone points used in the manufacture of coiled basketry at Taforalt, Morocco. These artefacts were found within the Gray Series deposits dating to between c. 15,000 and 12,000 years ago (Figure 4F). Similarly aged pointed and spatulate awls made on metapodial, or tibial bones of goat or gazelle—suitable for basket weaving—are found in contemporaneous Natufian contexts at Kebara (Turville-Petre 1932, p. 272), while Soffer (2004) has highlighted that a number of other bone implement forms may have functioned as weaving swords, weaving sticks, matting needles and netting gauges from Upper Paleolithic European contexts, including the Aurignacian at Vogelherd (Germany), Moravian Gravettian sites, and contemporary Russian sites (Soffer 2004). Stone (2010, 2011) likewise identified bone points exhibiting characteristic fiber working use-wear from Magdalenian sites in northern Spain. Finally, a possible bone awl of the size commonly used in weaving fiber baskets was found in c. 42,000-year-old levels at Riwi in northwestern Australia (Figure 4G; Langley et al. 2021a, p. 680), while the strong ethnographically observed connection between bone awls and basket-making in South America has been used to suggest the function of these pointed bone artefacts during the Terminal Pleistocene in Tierra del Fuego (see Bach et al. 2023).

Tools for Enacting Symbolic Behaviors

As noted in the introduction, the original conception of a bone tool did not account for objects that served a ‘non-utilitarian’ purpose. Reserving the word ‘tool’ for objects that helped in the performance of a physical activity allows ornaments and bones that were decorated with no obvious intended utilitarian purpose to be discussed separately for convenience. However, in as far as these objects of adornment still served a function (albeit aesthetic or symbolic) within the culture that made them, we consider it appropriate to include them here. Animals were not only a source of food and raw materials, but also the basis for many emblems, symbols, and myths (Boisvert et al. 2021; Choyke 2013; Ingold 1988). In some cases, the bones of specific animals would be selected for tool manufacture; the selection criteria being a function of the symbolic importance of the animal rather than of opportunity or performance mechanics. We see this aspect most clearly in the recent past (e.g., Gates St-Pierre et al. 2020) but the practice clearly had its genesis in the Pleistocene (e.g., Bradfield 2018; Desmond et al. 2018).

Information-Holding Tools

Perhaps owing to its association with living beings as well as its relative plasticity, bone served as a canvas for artistic expression throughout the Paleolithic period. The earliest identified engraved bone comes from Bilzingsleben in Germany and dates to around 370,000 years ago (Mania 1991, 18; Müller and Pasda 2011), while Płonka et al. (2024) have recently presented a bear radius from Middle Paleolithic (130,000–115,000 years old) levels at Dziadowa Skała, Poland, that has multiple deliberate incisions down one side (Figure 5A). In this same time period, two bones made from unweathered rib fragments and engraved with sets of sub-parallel lines were found at Lingjing, China, dating to between 125,000 and 105,000 years ago (Figure 5B; Li et al. 2019). The site of Prolom II in the Crimea is of similar age, and produced 360 fragments of anthropogenically splintered bone, some of which feature incised lines (Stepanchuk 1993). These incisions appear as sets of parallel lines or as lines radiating out from a point in a fan-shaped pattern. Similar incisions appear on a cave bear bone from the Mousterian site of Pešturina Cave in Serbia (Majkić et al. 2018). In all cases, the authors have interpreted the lines as evidence of symbolic behavior owing to their apparently careful placement. While attributing intentionality to incised lines is often problematic, owing to the fact that such groupings can, and often do, develop on bone cutting boards, the association of the engraved bones at Prolom II with unnaturally perforated phalanges lends credence to the symbolic interpretation; at least at this site. Even if the lines did not ‘mean’ anything, they at least demonstrate a rudimentary appreciation of pattern.

Sequentially notched bones have been found at several Middle Stone Age and terminal Pleistocene sites in Africa and beyond. The oldest such example appears in 80,000-year-old deposits at Apollo 11 Cave, Namibia, but the purpose of the notches was originally considered enigmatic (Vogelsang et al. 2010, p. 197). Beaumont and Bednarik (2013), however, concluded from their study of numerous African notched bones that in most cases they represent a form of Paleoart. The visual appeal created by the uniformity in the notching design on the baboon fibula from c. 40,000-year-old levels at Border Cave and other bones from c. 30,000-year-old levels at Sibudu, South Africa, has led to their interpretation as notational devices (d’Errico et al. 2012a, pp. 2492–2493, 2012b, pp. 13215–13218). Objects with sequential markings have purportedly been used to store and retrieve numerical information since at least 60,000 years ago at sites like Les Pradelles in France (d’Errico et al. 2017) and Cave of Hearths in South Africa (Mason 1988, p. 493). The visual consistency of sequential notches on a raven radius is also seen at the Mousterian site of Zaskalnaya VI in the Crimea, where they are interpreted as symbolic markings (Majkić et al. 2017). Notches of varying depth are found on worked bones in our study period at sites like Blombos Cave (Henshilwood and Sealy 1997), Ishango (Brooks and Smith 1987), Klasies River Main Site (Bradfield and Wurz 2020) and Kuumbi Cave (Langley et al. 2016b). Not all of these examples, however, are unequivocally symbolic, as use-wear has shown that, at least for some, a utilitarian (non-symbolic) interpretation may be more appropriate (d’Errico and Henshilwood 2007; Bradfield and Wurz 2020).

Incisions may be placed on bone for other reasons too. Engravings on two polished caprid astragali from the Terminal Pleistocene transition period at La Grotte de Remouchamps, Belgium, are thought to represent numerals from a quinary counting system (Dewez 1974). Based on ethnographic parallels, Dewez interprets these bones as possible gaming pieces or divination paraphernalia. We also see examples in the Eurasian Mesolithic where incised lines can be used as an anchorage device for hafting (Zhilin 2017, 2021), and much later in time, during the southern African Later Stone Age, where they served as marks of ownership (Wiessner 1983). Similar interpretations have been proffered onto early Holocene bone incisions throughout the world (e.g., Medina et al. 2022; Petrullo and Barich 2021). Of course, there are other examples which are clearly modified, but their use or meaning remain, nevertheless, enigmatic. One such example is a recently described giant deer phalanx found in Einhornhöhle in northern Germany. Here, some 51,000 years ago, a Neanderthal individual carefully engraved 10 straight lines at ninety-degree angles to one another into one of the sides of the bone (Figure 5C; Leder et al. 2021). Such attention to detail certainly points to a symbolic or at least aesthetic value to this piece.

Personal Adornment

Bones were also modified to serve as ornaments and other bodily decorations. Currently, the oldest bone ornament comes from Carpenter’s Gap 1 rockshelter in north western Australia (Bunuba Country), and dates to at least 46,000 years ago (Figure 5D; Langley et al. 2016c). This long piece of kangaroo fibula is covered in polish and ochre residues consistent with prolonged skin contact. While it is possible that this bone represents an awl used in the production of leather garments, comparison of its raw material (species and skeletal element), morphology, and distribution of use-wear and residues to ethnographically known awls and nose bones found that the Bunuba piece was most likely a nose bone. Nose bones are a common facial ornament across the Australian continent, being worn by men, women, and children according to local custom (Langley 2023, pp. 180–193). Outside of Australia, bone ornaments for piercings (including labrets) do not become common in the archaeological record until the Holocene period, though at sites where they have been identified insights into their wearers can be gained. For example, at Late Holocene sites in the La Plata Basin of South America, the size of the labrets suggests that they were worn by children (Acosta et al. 2024), thus adding an additional dimension to our understanding of the intersection between bone technology and human culture in this region. Similar studies of size in conjunction with use-wear analysis of possible bone ornaments for piercings may produce new insights into the wearers in more ancient contexts.

During the Mousterian and Châtelperronian periods in Europe, talons from raptors were targeted by Neanderthal communities and, based on cut marks and other surface modifications, likely used as pieces of personal adornment by these populations. Furthermore, cut marks found on wing bones suggests the removal of the long flight feathers, with those from raptors sporting black and white plumage of particular interest to the population collecting the feathers (Radovčić et al. 2015; Rodríguez-Hidalgo et al. 2019; Romandini et al. 2014, 2016).

Moving to Homo sapiens in Europe, comprehensive studies of Aurignacian and Gravettian ornaments utilized the diversity of bone beads and pendants along with those made on tooth, antler, ivory, and shell to suggest possible ethno-linguistic groupings (Baker et al. 2024; Vanhaeren and d’Errico 2006). Similar analysis of ornaments recovered from the later and richer Magdalenian assemblages have also proved useful in identifying social connections between geographically spread sites (e.g., Fuentes et al. 2019). Moving east, the Epipaleolithic Natufian culture of the Levant (c. 15,000–12,000 years ago) is similarly renowned for its rich bone industry, including bone beads made on gazelle phalanx and ‘pear-shaped’ pendants, which have been found in abundance at several sites, but curiously absent in others (Torres et al. 2020; Turville-Petre 1932). The Natufian, like the contemporaneous Magdalenian in Western Europe, regularly contain quotidian tools decorated with engravings, sculptures, and colorants. One example from the Natufian is a bone sickle-blade haft found at Kebara (Israel), which has a goat’s head design carved into it (Turville-Petre 1932). Grosman et al. (2016, pp. 21, 23) describe bone objects incised with a delicate geometric pattern of closed triangles at Nahal Ein Gev II – a pattern seen elsewhere, including at Hayonim Cave (Bar-Yosef and Belfer-Cohen 1999). Similarly, the European Magdalenian spearthrowers, spatulas, and projectiles frequently feature both geometric and figurative motifs (e.g., Fuentes et al. 2019; Rivero and Sauvet 2014).

On the other side of the globe, perforated bone pendants occur in abundance at Mid-Upper Paleolithic sites linked to the Beringian Refugium (Lbova 2010; Graf and Buvit 2017), while a bead made from a metapodial or proximal phalanx of a hare was recently found at the La Prele Mammoth Site in Converse County, Wyoming, (USA). This artefact, dated to ~12,940 BP, represents the first tangible evidence for the material exploitation of hares during the Clovis period (Surovell et al. 2024). Further south in Brazil, three giant sloth bones were discovered dating to between 26,000 and 19,000 years ago that were artificially modified by different tools and techniques and interpreted as suspended ornaments (Figure 5E; Pansani et al. 2023).

Not all bone tools were themselves the active component of symbolic material culture. Tattooing needles, for instance, were simple devices that imparted symbolically loaded cultural decorations onto a human canvas. While anthropomorphic art from Upper Paleolithic Europe suggests that tattooing may have been practiced from the earliest periods (e.g., Dutkiewicz et al. 2024; Renaut 2020; Schuster 1968/1969), identified tattooing tools from Pleistocene contexts globally are exceedingly rare. As highlighted by Deter-Wolf and Gillreath-Brown (2024), early identifications of possible tattooing implements were based primarily on macro-morphological assessments, which is too simplistic an approach to narrow down a sharply pointed object to just tattooing. Previously, acutely pointed bipoints dating to the Magdalenian (21,000–14,000 years ago) recovered from Mas d’Azil (Ariege) had been suggested as tattooing tools (Péquart and Péquart 1962), while several of the Middle Stone Age bone unipoints from Blombos are also suggested to perhaps have been utilized in such a fashion (Deter-Wolf 2013). As yet, the detailed microscopic work needed to support these suggestions have not been undertaken, and as such, these suggestions remain only that.

Musical Instruments

Bone and ivory forms the sole surviving medium of musical expression during the Stone Age. Bone flutes and whistles occur in much of Europe, from their earliest occurrence possibly at Divje Babe I, Slovenia (recently redated to c. 50,000 years ago; Turk et al. 2018; although the anthropogenesis of this specimen is highly contested [see d’Errico et al. 1998a, b]), to Davant Pau Cave, Spain, dated to 23,000 years ago (Ibáñez et al. 2015). They are most common, however, in the Upper Paleolithic of Europe, particularly the Aurignacian (see Buisson 1990; Meñéndez and García 1998; Morley 2005, 2013) and occur as far east as the Transbaikal region of Siberia (Lbova et al. 2012). These flutes are usually perforated with one or more holes and were commonly made from naturally hollow bird bones, although sometimes larger mammal bones and mammoth ivory were used (Figure 5F). The number of perforations also differs. The possible Divje Babe I specimen has three holes, while a vulture radius from Hohl Fels, Germany (35,000 years ago) has five, and a goose radius from Kamenka, Russia (40,000–38,000 years ago) has only one (Conard et al. 2009; Higham et al. 2012; Lbova et al. 2013). A well-known example of a swan bone flute comes from Geissenklösterle, Germany, and dates to 37,000–43,000 years ago (Conard et al. 2009; Hahn and Münzell 1995). Singly perforated pieces are typically referred to as whistles, with the perforation thought to have been used to modulate the pitch or to produce a syncopated rhythm (e.g., Ibáñez et al. 2015; Morley 2005). Curiously, similar artefacts from other parts of the world dating to this period are rare, although an example of a bone whistle turned up at Eynan-Mallaha (Israel), dating to the Final Natufian, c. 12,000 years ago (Davin et al. 2023).

Three other types of musical instruments made from bone that are sometimes found include the bullroarer, the spinning disk, and the rasp. A bullroarer is a flat, oblong, piece of bone, wood, or stone with a hole at one end, through which a string was attached (Dundes 1976; Morley 2003). A spinning disk has a similar construction but has two perforations in the middle (Kirby 2013). Both types of instruments have ethnohistoric correlates in various parts of the world. Among some Indigenous Australian cultures for instance, bullroarers were used in a variety of rituals to “create the voice of spirit beings,” whereas among the Malayans they were used to scare away animals (Morley 2005, p. 214). Bone bullroarers, sometimes elaborately decorated, have been recovered from several European Solutrean and Magdalenian sites (see Dauvais 1989; Morley 2005, pp. 215, 2013, pp. 105–107). A bullroarer and a spinning disk were identified from Later Stone Age (c. 9,000–6,000 years old) contexts at two sites in South Africa (Figure 5G; Kumbani et al. 2019).

The last item, bone rasps, are long pieces of bone with deep, well-spaced notches running along one or both sides. They are played like a violin bow by passing the rasp over another surface to produce a pattering or croaking sound. Mammoth bone rasps have been recovered from several Magdalenian sites, such as Pekarna in Moravia and Bruniquel in France (Huyge 1990). Lbova and colleagues (2012) estimate there to be at least 225 bone musical instruments across Eurasia dating to the Paleolithic.

Curiously, all varieties of bone musical instruments seem to disappear from the Eurasian archaeological record in the immediate Post-Glacial Period. Morley (2005) questions whether this absence is real or simply a product of misidentification in the literature. Such misidentification is a distinct possibility as the Matjes River rockshelter example in South Africa illustrates. Here, the bullroarer was originally misidentified as a pendant (Louw 1960) before use-wear shed light on its actual function. Owing to the relative scarcity of use-wear studies on bone tools from our study period it is possible that more bullroarers might be lurking in our museum collections under the moniker of pendant, or simply ‘perforated bone’.

The implications of musical instruments in the Paleolithic period, particularly if present among Neanderthal populations, are profound and speak to a sophisticated behavioral repertoire. Such behaviors seem to have been expressed primarily, if not exclusively, through the medium of hard animal tissues, like bone. However, as Lbova and colleagues (2012) rightly point out, musical behavior must necessarily have preceded the actual appearance of designed instruments. It is therefore likely that music had its genesis much earlier than the current artefactual record would suggest.

Discussion

Because of the near ubiquity of bone as a raw material across time and space, the study of bone tools and bone manufacturing technology can provide unique and valuable insights into past techno-economies that are complementary to more established avenues of material culture analysis. Indeed, studies of bone tool technology have revealed the richness and antiquity of material culture expressed through this medium (e.g., Langley 2023; Langley et al. 2016a; Zhang et al. 2000, 2018) and elucidated the trajectory along which bone tool technology has evolved (Ma and Doyon 2021). They have shown how bone-working was adopted into regional manufacturing traditions that were independent of other elements of material culture (d’Errico et al. 2012a) and highlighted possible past communication and exchange networks (Deacon 1992; Rabett and Piper 2012, pp. 48–49). Furthermore, because bone tools were more often used to work perishable materials, their study can provide unique insights into technologies, behaviors, and cognitive abilities that are not otherwise evident in the archaeological record (Bradfield 2020; Desmond 2022; Doyon et al. 2019; O’Connor et al. 2014; Parfitt and Bello 2024; Stone 2013). As such, when bone tool industries are taken into account, it becomes apparent that hominin technological evolution is far more complex and nuanced than a parochial consideration of any single material category would suggest.

It is difficult to convey in a single paper the richness and diversity of bone tool forms currently known from Stone Age (Pleistocene, Paleolithic) contexts around the globe. In this paper, we have attempted to synthesize the diverse range of technologies that were expressed through the medium of bone, from their first appearance through to about 8,000 years ago (Table 1). By prioritizing studies supported by use-wear analysis, and which are therefore more confident in their functional interpretations, we are able to demonstrate that there is now robust evidence that bone tools were being systematically produced from at least 1.5 million years ago, if not earlier, and that bone was deliberately and consistently selected as a raw material for hominin toolkits.

One of the themes we wished to explore in this paper is the role that worked bone technology played in the expansion of hominin economic and dietary resources. Use-wear evidence on bone tools from the Cradle of Humankind sites in South Africa suggests that these tools were used to dig in certain types of sediments, most likely to harvest underground plant storage organs or termites (Backwell and d’Errico 2001; Stammers 2018; d’Errico et al. 2022). That this tool form persisted unchanged for more than a million years suggests that its function was integrally linked to a particular species of hominin endemic to the Cradle landscape and/or an endemic food source. The sites with large bone tool assemblages are found predominantly to the north of the Bloubank River and are associated with Paranthropus robustus fossils. Currently, there is little evidence to suggest that there are any foodstuffs unique to the northern side of the river, nor would the ecosystem have been dramatically different at this time. Baker (2022, pp. 193–198) has hypothesized that the contemporaneity of early Homo and P. robustus would have necessitated the partitioning of the Cradle landscape to avoid or reduce resource competition. Whereas early Homo seem to have capitalized on lithic tools to increase the probability of scavenging success, P. robustus would have diversified their foraging behavior to include subterranean foods and entomophagy, something that is thus far not recorded for early Homo diets (Lüdecke et al. 2018; van Der Merwe et al. 2008). If bone tools were adopted for this purpose, it would explain their use-wear and distribution on the landscape.

The contra-positioning of this early expression of bone tool technology with contemporaneous bone working in East Africa, where bone was used predominantly to cleave meat, highlights the versatile application of bone technology to a variety of dietary procurement strategies. The realization that bone could be harnessed as a tool rather than simply as a source of marrow, as well as the bifacially knapped nature of some of these early bone tools from East Africa, indicates the early development of cognitive fluidity whereby hominins must have had an understanding of bone and stone fracturing properties and were able to fashion these tools according to a mental template (De la Torre et al. 2025; Rossano 2017).

The application of bone to the expansion of economic and dietary resources is seen again during the African Middle Stone Age when harpoons make their first appearance, and later small bipoints, that enabled a shift to incorporating aquatic resources (Yellen 1998). These Omega-rich foodstuffs were once thought to have contributed to the evolutionary development of the human brain (e.g., Broadhurst et al. 2002), though this over-emphasis has since been challenged (e.g., Lombard 2022). At about the same time, bow-and-arrow-technology is currently thought to have been invented (Lombard 2019), and bone seems to have been adopted just as much as stone for this toolkit. The application of mechanically assisted, ranged weapon systems fundamentally altered the hunting landscape and allowed early humans to access resources that would otherwise have been too dangerous to hunt, enabled decreased reliance on group hunting strategies, while also supporting the capture of smaller, fast-moving (and arboreal) prey that require weapons of greater speed and accuracy than a spear. This advancement in turn may have facilitated smaller group sizes and greater mobility. It is perhaps, then, not coincidental that these shifts are seen concomitant with a precocious florescence of cultural expression in Africa, around 80,000 to 60,000 years ago.

Coupled to the purposeful modification of bone to exploit different dietary resources is its use to create and modify other items of technology, such as stone tools. Use-wear bears witness to how, from the earliest times, bone was widely utilized as a soft hammer percussor to shape stone. As both a direct tool and also as an intermediary device used to refine other technologies, worked bone contributes to broader theoretical discussions around the evolution of technologies (and the human capacity for innovation) as they developed to meet the challenges of everyday life (Hutson et al. 2018a). From these initial uses by our earliest African ancestors, bone then continued to be integrated into the technological repertoire of diverse forms of humanity throughout the Stone Age across the globe. Ultimately, bone technologies supported our behavioral flexibility and adaptability to various and changing environments, playing a crucial role in the refinement of various tools and technologies, particularly from the Middle Stone Age onwards.

One of the advantages of bone tool studies is not what it may tell us about bone technology per se, but in what it may reveal about other technologies for which bone was but an instrument in their manufacture; technologies that are themselves highly perishable and not typically preserved in the archaeological record (O’Connor et al. 2014; Bradfield 2020; Houmard and Sidéra 2024a, b).
