These technologies and the complex human behaviors they signal can nevertheless preserve in the form of use-wear on the tools used in their production. We expect that with new traceological methods, we will gain increasingly detailed knowledge of when and where ‘soft materials’ were being processed and manipulated into material culture.

Another theme we wish to highlight is the role of bone technology in facilitating trans-continental migrations. Evidence for human dispersals and the role of technological adaptation strategies in that process have for so long relied almost exclusively on stone tools (e.g., Callaway 2011; Groucutt et al. 2015). Yet, we have seen how use-wear evidence found on bone eyed needles (for example) is rewriting what we know of the timing of human dispersals into high latitudes. The ability to stitch together animal skins and pelts facilitated the manufacture of clothing that provided warmth and protection, which in turn allowed people to migrate into colder climates. Similarly, bone implements were used to weave together plant fibers to make baskets, mats, and other paraphernalia that could be used to store and carry items needed to make long-distance journeys. The presence of twisted fiber technologies and carrying containers implies a profound understanding of our own human limitations, the cognitive ability to plan ahead, as well as a mathematical understanding of pairs, sets, and numbers—attributes that when found in association with early (~100,000-year-old) sites or species of hominin other than our own, highlight a level of cognition not previously recognized (Hardy et al. 2010; Suddendorf et al. 2020). As such, these attributes may signal more than just the development of ever increasingly complex technologies, but the evolution of a whole range of psychosocial processes, which facilitated the rich cultural experiences of the modern day (Gilligan 2024).

Indeed, bones hold significant symbolic and practical value among diverse cultures where, at least in the more recent periods that fall outside of our current focus, they are used in various ritual performances, including divination, ancestor veneration, funerary rites, and even components in artistic dance and music (Altamirano García and García 2018; Baron et al. 2022; Muleka 2023). The plasticity of bone makes it an ideal medium on which to execute carvings and engravings, while its relative hardness makes it more durable than wood. These properties make bone a fruitful medium for exploring concepts of materiality and entanglement within the archaeological record (sensu Der and Fernandini 2016; Hodder 1982, 2012).

We have seen how bone itself was used as a canvas to convey decorative and perhaps symbolic information (Leder et al. 2021). These objects are intimately entwined and entangled with early expressions of culture and with cognitive developments. Perhaps, as Ingold (1988) has noted, bone, coming from a once-living creature, would have been imbued with an intrinsic symbolic importance to early humans—a reminder of their own mortality, perhaps; or a link to the animal world on which humans both depend and over which they would eventually acquire mastery. These concepts are perhaps best highlighted in the many examples of musical instruments fashioned from bone, such as flutes, whistles, spinning discs and rasps. With the innate potential of bone as a medium for symbolic conveyance and the increasing application of sophisticated use-wear methodologies, it is perhaps no surprise that additional musical instruments and decorative objects are increasingly being recognized from Paleolithic contexts.

Although not inclusive of all the sites which have produced Stone Age bone artefacts, Figure 1 reveals geographical concentrations of bone-working technology. This distribution is in part a product of the differential timing of the peopling of the world, with South America and Oceania necessarily having fewer sites dating to our focus period than Africa and Eurasia. But it also reflects the traditional focus of researchers on Europe and sub-Saharan Africa and the neglect of osseous technologies in favor of their lithic counterparts in our most ancient archaeological records. It likely also reflects the harsh realities of organic preservation in areas of the global south (Langley et al. 2011), though we should be careful not to forget these regions completely as continuing work is resulting in finds which fill in important gaps (as evident in the preceding sections). Indeed, research in the Far East (particularly China) through to Oceania and across to the New World is increasingly reporting new discoveries of early bone technologies, and we expect these finds are just the tip of the iceberg (Figure 2).

As much as worked bone is subject to biodegradation, making them relatively rare artefacts, they are perhaps not as rare as often supposed. Fragments of ad hoc bone tools (pieces of bone that show signs of scraping and differential polish distribution) that had for decades lain unrecognized among the unmodified fauna, have been discovered from Howiesons Poort levels (c. 65,000 to 46,000) at Klasies River Main site in South Africa (Cleminson et al. 2025). Similarly, bone tool fabrication debitage is something seldom sought after by faunal analysts, whose primary concern is the taxonomic identification of the ‘economic’—that is, food—faunal remains. As such, even in the absence of finished and utilized bone tools, we may find evidence for their presence in the fabrication debris left behind (Christensen and Goutas 2018); an area of analysis which may bear promising and unexpected results if given enough academic attention. Consequently, many unrecognized bone tools may already be lurking in our museums and storerooms awaiting dedicated use-wear analysis to reveal their true identity.

Returning to the tendency of grouping all bone artefact forms into a single ‘bone tool’ category for discussion in grand narratives of human evolution, this situation is perhaps partly the fault of bone artefact analysts themselves as the often nebulous and unhelpful morpho-functional nomenclature by which bone tools have traditionally been referred can lead to the misidentification of the actual function of a bone tool (and the consequent interpretative garden path this leads down), not to mention the obscuration of functional diversity within a particular morpho-typological category.

Coupled to this problem is the tendency, particularly in Europe, to lump together different hard animal materials (bone and antler and sometimes ivory) into the generic term, osseous, which may obscure important techno-cultural differences. Certainly, this grouping together of Paleolithic-aged antler and bone (along with ivory) projectile technologies proved an issue for determining the presence and role of bone artefacts for this paper. We encourage future researchers working with such mixed assemblages to not only determine the raw material of all pieces (which most analysts would already do), but also consider and report on the differential use of osseous raw materials in each assemblage.

Indeed, one of the challenges to any functional interpretation is the reliability of the empirical data; in this case, primarily the use-wear evidence preserved on an artifact's surface. The more so the older the artefact and the greater its exposure to taphonomic factors. Notwithstanding the large corpus of experimental referents now published (e.g., Buc 2011; Bradfield 2015a; Desmond et al. 2021; Desmond 2022; Griffitts 1997; Orłowska and Osipowicz 2017), the subjective nature of the inferences drawn from observations, a lack of standardized descriptive nomenclature, and the problem of equifinality have occasioned the use of an ever-growing variety of surface imaging and measurement techniques (Marreiros et al. 2015; Bradfield 2016b). Yet, despite significant advances in the application of analytics like surface roughness analysis (Lesnik 2011; Martisius et al. 2018, 2020a, b; Martisius 2022) use-wear interpretations still remain largely interpretative (Bradfield 2022; van Gijn 2014). We would argue that dual technological and use-wear analysis remains the best approach to interpreting the evidence contained in the worked bone artefact category.

When considered in tandem with lithic studies, worked bone research – and that of all other hard animal materials – has the potential to provide complementary lines of evidence that broaden our evolutionary understanding of technological change and cultural expression in the past. Indeed, some lines of evidence provided by bone material culture is often completely lacking in the lithic record simply because stone tools were used for different tasks to their bone counterparts. As such, the information yielded by bone tools is not merely an augmentation of existing knowledge provided by other cultural materials, but a whole avenue of inquiry in itself. Certain technologies, and by extension the associated human behaviors, were expressed primarily through the medium of bone tools through the medium of bone tools—notwithstanding the possible employment of wood, which survives significantly less well (Aranguren et al. 2018; Barham et al. 2023). Musical instruments and personal adornments are obvious cases in point, but they are not the only examples. In North Africa, the production of bone tools is shown to correlate with changes in human behaviors that led to increased sedentism, highlighting the potential of bone tools to provide insights into broad scale techno-cultural negotiations that are independent of lithic and ceramic traditions (Desmond et al. 2018). Similarly, in South Africa, bone tool technology has been shown to have had its own independent regional and temporal rates of change, both in terms of manufacturing technology and finished products (d’Errico et al. 2012a).

Moving forward, we hope to see many more studies of both newly recovered and long-curated single bone artefacts and assemblages. Broadening the membership base of organizations like the Worked Bone Research Group and encouraging greater intercontinental communication and sharing of research, while increasing experimental and ethnographic reference samples, standardizing methodological analyses and descriptive reporting will greatly facilitate the construction of new understandings of these animal-based technologies. Future work in bone tool studies, while continuing to focus on a functional assessment of individual artifacts, should also seek to integrate these datasets into existing techno-culture models so as to provide a fuller, less skewed picture of the past. This aspect is particularly important in Stone Age archaeology where the entire framework through which we understand the past is governed by reconstructions of changes and continuities in lithic production strategies, and in more recent periods, where ceramic production and style are used to define entire cultures. It will only be with these careful considerations of non-stone technologies—and the adding of that information to our knowledge of stone technologies—that our understanding of human behavioral and cultural diversity throughout our deep past will be broadened.

Conclusion

Bone artefacts and assemblages provide an additional dimension to our understanding of the intersection between technology, culture, and the environment. Indeed, the emergence of Homo sapiens in Pleistocene Africa is associated with a reconfiguration of technology, including the use of bone to make specialized tools that were likely expressed as discreet technical traditions, independent of stone tool technology (d’Errico et al. 2012a, 2020, pp. 21–22, 2022; Hallett et al. 2021). Some of these material expressions had precursors in the Earlier Stone Age/Lower Paleolithic and likely followed their own technological trajectories (Backwell and d’Errico 2003; d’Errico and Backwell 2007). As such, with so much work waiting to be done both within specialist studies of bone artefacts and the integration of these data into broader constructions of our species development, we truly are only at the beginning of what bone tools can tell us about the human story.
